title: A Multimethod Approach for Assessing Groundwater Flow Systems Dynamics Using Surface Indicators
content:
ABSTRACT

The study presents an integrated approach to the natural environment, using surface indicators in a karst system. The objective was to identify vegetation and soil characteristics in karst groundwater recharge and discharge areas and to understand groundwater's role as a landscape-shaping agent, given the contrasting characteristics between recharge and discharge areas. This study involved detailed fieldwork, physicochemical soil characterization and assessment of vegetation structure parameters. The results reveal that recharge zones exhibit higher diversity and species richness (H = 3.60; D = 11.94) than discharge zones (H = 3.08; D = 7.59). Soils in recharge areas are less developed (≤ 10 cm), have higher organic matter (OM) content (> 30%), lower electrical conductivity (EC) (≤ 300 μS/cm), and lower pH (6.44 to 7.65). In contrast, discharge zone soils tend to be more developed and exhibit characteristics that vary with the associated discharge type. In Ca-HCO3 discharge, soil depth is ≥ 105 cm, pH of 7.27 to 7.65, OM content ≤ 19%, and EC levels ≤ 1043 μS/cm. In Ca-SO4 discharges, soils are ≥ 102 cm deep, with a pH between 6.68 and 7.69, OM content ≤ 15%, and EC levels ≤ 2727 μS/cm. Additionally, specific plant species were identified as indicators of recharge areas, such as Quercus xalapensis, Harpalyce arborescens, Solenandra mexicana and Casearia laetioides; in Ca-HCO3 discharges, Salix humboldtiana and Enterolobium cyclocarpum; while species found in Ca-SO4 discharges included Inga vera, Guazuma ulmifolia and Leucaena leucocephala. The research demonstrates that indicators such as vegetation and soil types can effectively differentiate between recharge and discharge zones based on their contrasting characteristics.
